target: Agent 1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would give many voters scheduling flexibility and reduce work/school-based barriers.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably give paid time off in the private sector, so many retail and service workers—especially low-income workers—would still have to work on Election Day and would not gain meaningful scheduling flexibility.

target: Agent 1’s broader assumption that a holiday would reduce barriers enough to increase turnout substantially.
objection: If low-income workers still must work, then the holiday does not meaningfully reduce the work-based voting barriers faced by the voters most affected, so it is unlikely to raise turnout in a significant way.

target: Agent 1’s claim that school closures and holiday framing make Election Day a broadly helpful scheduling reform.
objection: Because some low-income families would still face work obligations, a holiday can disadvantage low-income voters relative to people with more flexible jobs, and an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: Agent 2’s claim that the lack of federal paid time off means a holiday would not create real scheduling flexibility for low-income workers.
objection: Even if federal law does not require private employers to give paid time off, many businesses still reduce hours or close on federal holidays, which can create actual non-work time for low-income workers in retail and service jobs.

target: Agent 1’s claim that reduced business hours on holidays would help low-income workers vote.
objection: Federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or give paid leave, and many retail and service workplaces are likely to stay open and keep employees working, so the holiday would still not reliably create non-work time for hourly workers.

target: Agent 2’s assumption that only employer closure or paid leave matters for low-income families.
objection: Even if some employers remain open, a holiday would still reduce school and caregiving scheduling barriers because schools close and families gain daytime flexibility, helping low-income voters who are constrained by children’s schedules.

target: Agent 2’s claim that an Election Day holiday would mainly shift costs onto workers without helping them.
objection: For hourly workers, many workplaces reduce hours or close on federal holidays, so the holiday can create real non-work windows and reduce work-based voting barriers rather than merely shifting the cost of voting.

target: Agent 1’s claim that reduced hours or closures on holidays reliably create paid time to vote.
objection: Even if some workplaces reduce hours or close, federal holiday status does not ensure hourly workers get paid leave; many may still face an unpaid or partially unpaid time-off situation, so the wage/time barrier remains.

target: Agent 2’s claim that holiday status is too weak to matter for hourly workers.
objection: If workplaces reduce hours or close, hourly workers’ schedules actually track those changes, so the holiday can create practically meaningful non-work time windows that directly reduce wage-loss voting barriers.

target: Agent 2’s claim that school closure is not a meaningful benefit for low-income parents.
objection: A holiday also reduces school and caregiving scheduling barriers because schools close and family routines are less demanding, which gives parents more time and flexibility to vote.

target: Agent 1’s claim that school closure meaningfully helps low-income parents vote.
objection: For many low-income families, school closure does not remove caregiving burdens; it can require arranging substitute care that costs time or money, so a holiday may not reliably reduce and can even increase those barriers.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that school closure solves the main voting problem for low-income voters.
objection: For low-income voters whose main constraint is limited availability during Election Day work hours, school closure does not create a feasible voting window if they still cannot take time off from work.
